prompt: A non-AAA lab router already has SSHv2, keys and a local username. Which two commands under every VTY range require local login and allow only SSH? (Choose two.)
options: transport input telnet ssh
transport input ssh
password Readiness-Lab-45
login local
ip ssh version 2
explanation: `transport input ssh` limits remote access to SSH, and `login local` uses the local username database. An access-class can add a source restriction.

whyWrong.2: A line password does not use the local username database.
whyWrong.4: `ip ssh version 2` is a global command and is already present.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 SSH state
exhibit.text:
SSH Disabled
Please create RSA keys to enable SSH.
Configured VTY transport: ssh
Configured authentication: login local

prompt: A fresh SW1 has a hostname, domain name, local user and SSH-only VTY settings, but the output reports no RSA key. What supplies the missing prerequisite?
options: Replace the local account with a VTY line password
Reapply the SSH-only transport setting on the VTYs
Generate a supported 2048-bit RSA server key pair
Increase the VTY idle timeout to keep the session open
explanation: The output shows the SSH server key is missing. Generate a 2048-bit RSA key pair, then verify SSHv2 and test a fresh login.

whyWrong.0: A line password cannot supply a server key.
whyWrong.1: The transport setting exists and does not create a key.
whyWrong.3: An idle timeout does not create an SSH key.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 channel state
exhibit.text:
Po1(SD) LACP Fa0/23(I) Fa0/24(I)
SW1 members: channel-group 1 mode passive
SW2 members: channel-group 1 mode passive

prompt: Both switches have working trunk ports in channel group 1, but both ends use LACP passive. Which change starts negotiation while keeping LACP?
options: Set both ends to channel-group 1 mode on
Set one end to channel-group 1 mode active
Set the native VLAN to 1 at both ends
Set the port-channel to spanning-tree portfast
explanation: LACP passive only responds, so at least one end must be active.

whyWrong.0: `on` is a static bundle, not LACP.
whyWrong.2: The native VLAN does not start LACP.
whyWrong.3: PortFast is for edge ports, not inter-switch links.

prompt: Both switches use priority 32768 in VLANs 10, 20, 99 and 999, and SW2 wins by MAC address. Which SW1 command makes it root in all four VLANs against default-priority peers?
options: spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 priority 32768
spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary
spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 root primary
spanning-tree vlan 10,20,99,999 priority 61440
explanation: `root primary` lowers the bridge priority below the default peers, typically to 24576 on Catalyst. Check the elected root afterward.

whyWrong.0: Keeping 32768 leaves the MAC address as the tie-breaker.
whyWrong.1: VLAN 1 is not one of the four VLANs.
whyWrong.3: A higher number is less preferred.

exhibit.title: Representative SW1 trunk excerpt
exhibit.text:
Port   Status     Native   Allowed VLANs
Gi0/1  trunking   999      10,99,999
Po1    trunking   999      10,20,99,999

prompt: A guest on SW2 VLAN 20 needs DHCP from R1 behind SW1 Gi0/1. Its access VLAN and Po1 are fine, but no lease arrives, and R1 Gi0/0.20 is up/up. What interrupts the path?
options: VLAN 20 is excluded from the router-facing trunk
VLAN 999 needs an IPv4 address on the switch
The router needs a DHCP helper to its own pool
The guest VLAN must be the trunk native VLAN
explanation: SW1 Gi0/1 does not allow VLAN 20, so the tagged guest traffic never reaches R1. An up/up subinterface does not check the switch's allowed list.

whyWrong.1: The unused native VLAN needs no address for tagged VLAN 20.
whyWrong.2: R1 is already the DHCP server, so it needs no helper to itself.
whyWrong.3: VLAN 20 can be tagged while another VLAN is native.

prompt: R1 Gi0/0.20 must route tagged VLAN 20 as 10.10.20.1/24. The parent is up and the switch trunk carries VLAN 20. Which two subinterface commands are needed? (Choose two.)
options: encapsulation dot1Q 20
switchport access vlan 20
ip helper-address 10.10.20.1
ip ospf network point-to-point
explanation: `encapsulation dot1Q 20` binds the VLAN tag and `ip address` gives the gateway.

whyWrong.1: A routed subinterface uses encapsulation, not switchport commands.
whyWrong.3: A helper to the same router is not needed.
whyWrong.4: An OSPF network type supplies neither tag nor address.

exhibit.title: Representative both transit interfaces
exhibit.text:
R1: Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type POINT_TO_POINT, Hello 10, Dead 40
R2: Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Hello 10, Dead 40
R1 neighbor 2.2.2.2: FULL
Expected remote LAN route: absent

prompt: The two ends of an OSPF transit show this state. The LANs are enabled in area 0, but routes are missing. What should you fix first?
options: Different local OSPF process identifiers
Different IPv4 administrative distances
Different OSPF network types on the link
Different learned external route metrics
explanation: The output shows mismatched OSPF network types on the link. Mismatched types can stop route calculation even when the neighbor state is FULL.

whyWrong.0: Process IDs are local and do not need to match.
whyWrong.1: No administrative distance difference is shown.
whyWrong.3: No external metric difference is shown.

prompt: R1's pool STAFF uses network 10.10.10.0/24 on a directly attached VLAN. Reserve .1 to .49 and give clients gateway .1. Which two additions meet this? (Choose two.)
options: ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.1 10.10.10.49 in global mode
ip helper-address 10.10.10.1 on the client interface
network 10.10.10.50 255.255.255.0 in the pool
default-router 10.10.10.1 in the pool
ip dhcp excluded-address 10.10.10.50 10.10.10.254 globally
explanation: The global exclusion reserves .1 to .49 and `default-router` supplies the gateway. Clients lease .50 to .254.

whyWrong.1: A local server needs no relay to itself.
whyWrong.2: The pool already defines the /24 network.
whyWrong.4: That excludes the client range instead of .1 to .49.

prompt: R1's external ping uses source 10.255.12.1. R2 PAT permits only 10.10.10.0/24 and 10.10.20.0/24, and the ISP has no private return routes. Clients work. Which test uses an eligible source?
options: Add a default route on the clients toward R2 directly
Ping from R1 with source 10.10.10.1 and inspect R2 NAT
Mark R1’s transit as outside to create another translator
Change R2’s selector to permit every source without review
explanation: Source 10.10.10.1 is inside the PAT selector and crosses R2's inside and outside path. Comparing it with the transit-sourced test shows why the source matters.

whyWrong.0: The clients already use the correct gateway and work.
whyWrong.2: A second translator is not needed for this comparison.
whyWrong.3: Permitting every source changes the design instead of testing it.

prompt: GUEST-IN is inbound on the guest subinterface. Staff echo requests reach guests, but guest echo replies are dropped. New guest echo requests to staff must stay denied. What change fits?
options: Permit guest-to-staff ICMP echo-reply before the deny
Move the ACL to the staff subinterface inbound
Replace the final permit with permit icmp any any
Permit guest-to-staff ICMP echo before the deny
explanation: The guest reply enters the guest subinterface, so permit guest-to-staff echo-reply before the deny. New echo requests still match the deny, and the ACL does not track state.

whyWrong.1: Moving the list changes which traffic is filtered and breaks the guest-source policy.
whyWrong.2: A later entry cannot override the earlier deny.
whyWrong.3: Echo is the request type that must stay denied.

prompt: With `logging trap warnings`, which message is forwarded to the remote server?
options: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN
%LINK-5-CHANGED
%LINK-3-UPDOWN
explanation: Warnings is severity 4, so levels 0 to 4 are forwarded and 5 to 7 are not. %LINK-3-UPDOWN is severity 3.

whyWrong.2: Severity 5 is above the threshold.

spec.title: Branch, HQ and ISP
spec.caption: R1 Gi0/1 and R2 Gi0/0 share area 0; the ISP uses a static route relationship.

prompt: R1 and R2 use passive-interface default and enable OSPF on their LANs and the shared transit. Only the R1 to R2 link should form an adjacency. Which two interfaces need to be non-passive? (Choose two.)
options: R1 GigabitEthernet0/0.10
R1 GigabitEthernet0/1
R2 GigabitEthernet0/2
R2 GigabitEthernet0/0
R2 GigabitEthernet0/1
explanation: The transit is R1 Gi0/1 and R2 Gi0/0. The LAN interfaces stay passive while their prefixes are still advertised.

whyWrong.0: The staff subinterface should not form a neighbor.
whyWrong.2: The HQ server interface should stay passive.
whyWrong.4: The ISP is not an OSPF peer.

exhibit.title: Representative R1 default route
exhibit.text:
O*E2 0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] via 10.255.12.2
R2 design sets external metric 10 explicitly.

prompt: R1 learns an OSPF default from R2, which must advertise it only while its static default through 203.0.113.2 exists. Which settings do this?
options: An OSPF network statement plus passive-interface default
A static default plus an OSPF router-id statement
An OSPF network statement plus a NAT overload rule
A static default plus default-information originate without always
explanation: The static default is the route, and `default-information originate` without `always` advertises a default only while that route exists.

whyWrong.0: A network statement does not create a default route.
whyWrong.1: A router ID does not originate a default.
whyWrong.2: Neither a network statement nor NAT creates a default.

prompt: Guest gateway and external requests increment unintended line 35, while DHCP works. The policy should permit both requests and deny guest-to-staff. Which repair keeps the rest of the policy?
options: Remove sequence 35 within GUEST-IN
Detach GUEST-IN from the subinterface
Clear every dynamic NAT entry on R2
Replace the guest subnet’s default gateway
explanation: The broad deny at sequence 35 matches the guest packets before the intended entries. Remove only that sequence.

whyWrong.1: Detaching the list removes the required restrictions.
whyWrong.2: Clearing NAT does not remove the ACL deny.

prompt: DHCP moved to 10.255.20.10 with a correct staff pool and return route, and R1 has no helper on client-facing Gi0/0.10. What forwards the VLAN's requests to the new server?
options: Add ip helper-address 10.255.20.10 to R2’s server-facing interface
Add ip helper-address 10.255.20.10 to R1 Gi0/0.10
Re-create a competing staff DHCP pool on R1 itself
Set the client’s DNS option to the new DHCP server address
explanation: Put the helper where the client broadcast arrives: R1's staff subinterface. The relay sets giaddr to the staff gateway, so the server picks the right pool.

whyWrong.0: The server-facing interface does not receive the client broadcast.
whyWrong.2: A local pool on R1 changes the intended design.
whyWrong.3: A DNS option does not enable relay.

prompt: GUEST-IN permits guests to ping their gateway 10.10.20.1. R1 must accept SSH only from 10.10.10.0/24 and still allow the guest ping. Which control fits?
options: Apply a deny ip any any rule inbound on the guest subinterface
Remove the IP address from the guest gateway subinterface
Apply a staff-source standard ACL with access-class on all VTY lines
Mark the staff subinterface as a passive OSPF interface
explanation: An access-class on the VTY lines restricts SSH client sources independently of interface traffic. Keep local login and SSH-only transport.

whyWrong.0: A deny ip any any also blocks the permitted guest ping.
whyWrong.1: Removing the gateway address breaks the guest design.
whyWrong.3: A passive OSPF interface does not control SSH access.

prompt: Two 100 Mb/s members carry Po1. One is shut, Po1 stays up and a new guest HTTP request works. What does this support?
options: The channel now provides one 100 Mb/s member path; interruption and application performance must be observed
Each surviving flow retains 200 Mb/s because Po1 still has two configured members
Every packet took the failed member and was retransmitted without any delay
The test proves the branch can tolerate loss of the entire access switch
explanation: One member keeps a path up but halves the capacity. A successful request does not measure loss, delay or switch-level resilience.

whyWrong.1: A down member adds no capacity.
whyWrong.2: The result says nothing about per-packet handling or lossless failover.
whyWrong.3: Only a member link failed, not a whole switch.

prompt: Two guests in VLAN 20 talk directly through SW2, and GUEST-IN is only inbound on R1 Gi0/0.20. What should the acceptance record say about guest-to-guest isolation?
options: The router ACL blocks the traffic because both hosts have a guest source address
The router ACL is not traversed by ordinary same-subnet switching; this requirement is not implemented
The implicit deny blocks the traffic as soon as SW2 learns both source MACs
Adding another deny to the same router ACL will make SW2 inspect those frames
explanation: Same-subnet frames are switched in the VLAN and never reach the router ACL, so the requirement is not implemented. It needs a separate design such as client isolation.

whyWrong.0: The ACL only sees traffic that crosses the router.
whyWrong.2: The router's implicit deny is not a switch forwarding rule.
whyWrong.3: More entries on an untraversed ACL change nothing.

prompt: Which next step best isolates the guest failure without changing a working path?
options: Broaden NAT-LANS to permit any source because at least one application failed
Compare the guest DNS setting and a fresh lookup with the DNS server record
Replace the OSPF default because named and numeric URLs use separate routes
Clear every PAT entry because a successful numeric request cannot use PAT
explanation: The guest reaches the external service by address, so the failing step is name resolution. Check the guest DNS setting and a fresh lookup first.

whyWrong.0: The numeric request already shows NAT works for the guest.
whyWrong.2: Names resolve before IP forwarding, so the default route is not implicated.
whyWrong.3: A working numeric request shows PAT works, so do not clear sessions.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
Guest: http://198.51.100.10 loads the expected page; http://portal.capstone.test fails to resolve.
Staff: both URLs load.
R2: a fresh guest TCP/80 translation appears during the numeric request.

prompt: Which action fixes the missing return path and keeps client-facing OSPF interfaces passive?
options: Make every client-facing interface nonpassive so endpoints can form neighbors
Extend PAT to HQ traffic so the route advertisement no longer matters
Enable the staff interface in area 0 on R1 and verify R2 learns the staff prefix
Rebuild the transit adjacency because FULL requires every LAN route to be present
explanation: A passive LAN must still be enabled in OSPF for its prefix to be advertised. The staff interface is absent, so R2 lacks the staff route. Enable it in area 0, leave it passive and retest.

whyWrong.0: Hosts do not form OSPF adjacencies, and removing passive does not select an interface.
whyWrong.1: Extending PAT avoids the routing requirement instead of meeting it.
whyWrong.3: FULL describes database sync with one peer, not that every interface is selected.

exhibit.title: Authored evidence for this case
exhibit.text:
R1–R2: FULL; matching area, timers and point-to-point type.
R1 route: HQ 10.255.20.0/24 via R2.
R1 OSPF-enabled interfaces: Gi0/1 and Gi0/0.20 only; passive-interface default.
R2: guest 10.10.20.0/24 learned; no staff-prefix route; lookup for 10.10.10.50 selects the ISP default.
Staff ping to HQ fails; guest-to-HQ policy is intentionally denied.

prompt: Guest HTTPS to HQ host 10.255.20.10 must be permitted while other guest-to-HQ traffic stays denied. GUEST-IN has sequence 60 denying guests to 10.255.0.0/16. Which change and test meet this?
options: Insert a TCP destination-443 permit before sequence 60; test guest HTTPS and a still-denied guest HQ ping
Append a TCP destination-443 permit after sequence 60; test only the new entry’s configuration
Insert permit ip to the HQ host before sequence 60; test only a successful guest ping
Permit TCP source port 443 before sequence 60; test a guest request whose source port is ephemeral
explanation: A specific permit placed before the broader deny admits only that service. Test guest HTTPS and a guest HQ ping that stays denied.

whyWrong.1: A permit after sequence 60 is never reached.
whyWrong.2: `permit ip` admits other protocols, including the ping that must stay blocked.
whyWrong.3: Guest HTTPS has destination port 443, not source port 443.

prompt: Staff moved from 10.10.10.0/24 to 10.20.10.0/24. A client reaches all management addresses and external HTTP, and SSH keys and accounts are healthy, but MGMT-SOURCES on every device still permits only 10.10.10.0/24. What fixes this?
options: Replace the local account on R1 and use the old staff gateway as the SSH source
Remove every VTY source filter permanently and rely on successful authentication
Change the NAT selector to translate staff SSH into the old subnet
Update MGMT-SOURCES on all four managed devices; test fresh staff logins and a denied guest login
explanation: Routing and SSH are healthy, so the stale source policy is the fault. Update MGMT-SOURCES on all four managed devices, then test staff and guest logins.

whyWrong.0: An account is not missing, and the old subnet is no longer staff.
whyWrong.1: Removing the filter drops the staff-only requirement.
whyWrong.2: The external PAT rule does not repair the VTY source policy.

prompt: SW1 at 10.10.99.11 reaches HQ through R1/R2. R2 translates only 10.10.10.0/24 and 10.10.20.0/24, and the ISP has no route to 10.10.99.0/24. Why does SW1's external ping fail?
options: The switch lacks a usable gateway for all remote subnets
The HQ interface needs to be marked as NAT outside
The SVI cannot originate a packet to a routed destination
Its source is untranslated and the private return route is absent
explanation: The PAT selector does not match the management subnet, so the packet leaves untranslated. The ISP has no return route to a private source.

whyWrong.0: The HQ test uses the same gateway and works.
whyWrong.1: Marking the HQ segment outside changes the NAT boundary.
whyWrong.2: A management SVI can originate routed traffic.

prompt: In the capstone design, which VLAN is the management VLAN?
options: VLAN 10
VLAN 20
VLAN 99
VLAN 999
explanation: The design uses staff VLAN 10, guest VLAN 20, management VLAN 99 and unused native VLAN 999.

whyWrong.3: VLAN 999 is the unused native VLAN.

prompt: Which device holds the static default toward the simulated ISP and performs interface PAT?
options: SW1
SW2
R1
R2
explanation: R2 has the static default toward the ISP and performs interface PAT for the two client subnets. R1 provides the VLAN gateways and DHCP.

whyWrong.0: SW1 is a switch and the intended STP root.
whyWrong.2: R1 provides the VLAN gateways and DHCP pools.

prompt: Which switch is the intended Rapid PVST+ root in the capstone?
options: SW1
SW2
R1
R2
explanation: SW1 is the intended Rapid PVST+ root. SW1 and SW2 form LACP Port-channel1.

whyWrong.2: R1 is a router, not an STP root.
whyWrong.3: R2 is a router, not an STP root.

prompt: How does the capstone guest ACL treat return traffic?
options: It tracks sessions and allows returns automatically
It does not track sessions
It tracks only TCP sessions
It tracks sessions only for DHCP
explanation: The guest ACL does not track sessions, so it needs explicit entries for return traffic such as echo replies.

whyWrong.0: A standard extended ACL is stateless.
whyWrong.2: The ACL tracks no TCP sessions.
whyWrong.3: The ACL tracks no DHCP sessions.
